Lessons.Title: Comparing Graphs
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: compare two functions representing the same input-output quantities, identify intersections where A(t)=B(t), interpret A(t)>B(t) and compare rates of change with correct units. Independently authored Edulytiks lesson aligned with Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition Unit 4 Lesson 9, https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/4/9/preparation.html and student activities https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/students/1/4/9/index.html (CC BY 4.0). The source compares population and media trends; our separate data are a new mathematical model, not those observed records.

Original fictional two savings accounts: account A starts with $10 and adds $4 each week, so A(t)=10+4t; account B starts with $2 and adds $6 weekly, so B(t)=2+6t, for t≥0 whole weeks. At week0 A has more; at week4 they agree at $26; after week4 B becomes larger. The mathematical graph comprises two straight lines, but realistic deposits occur at discrete whole-week times.

An intersection of the graphs identifies a shared output at the SAME input. Solve 10+4t=2+6t to obtain t=4 and output26. A(2)=18 exceeds B(2)=14, whereas B(6)=38 exceeds A(6)=34. Comparing slope alone does not prove which account has greater balance at every time because starting amounts differ.

Student activity: graph both lines on common time/balance axes, label their intersection and relative position before/after, translate symbolic comparisons into everyday language, and consider how to change deposit amounts to move the crossing. Teacher-scored rubric (0–2 each, max 8): accurate shared-axis graph, checked comparisons and intersection, correct rate/intercept interpretation, and justified contextual explanation.

KeyConcepts.Title: Compare outputs
KeyConcepts.Definition: A(t)>B(t) means A has the larger output at the same input t.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use the same x coordinate and units for both functions.

KeyConcepts.Title: Intersection
KeyConcepts.Definition: A(t)=B(t) is solved by the input coordinates where the two graphs meet.

KeyConcepts.Title: Different average rates
KeyConcepts.Definition: The rate and starting value together determine which function is larger.
KeyConcepts.Example: A adds $4/week but B adds $6/week after a smaller start.

WorkedExamples.Title: Find the crossing input
WorkedExamples.Question: For A(t)=10+4t and B(t)=2+6t, find A(t)=B(t).
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the exact first-party function definition and independently verify each substitution, graph feature and domain.
Steps: Interpret as equal balances after four weeks.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare before the crossing
WorkedExamples.Question: Compare A(2) and B(2).
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the exact first-party function definition and independently verify each substitution, graph feature and domain.
Steps: Since18>14, A has more savings at week2.
Week2 is before the equality at week4.
WorkedExamples.Check: Both evaluations use the same week2 input.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare after the crossing
WorkedExamples.Question: Compare values and rates at week6.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the exact first-party function definition and independently verify each substitution, graph feature and domain.
Steps: B leads by $4 despite starting $8 behind.
B grows $2/week faster, so the difference changes by $2 per week.
WorkedExamples.Check: At week4 difference0, two weeks later difference4.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Comparing A(2) with B(6) as if same-time outputs
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Inputs differ so the comparison does not answer which is greater at a particular week.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assuming the function with higher rate starts higher
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Slope does not determine initial value.

SummaryPoints: Comparing functions uses common inputs, units and correctly labelled graphs.
A(t)=B(t) gives an intersection input; the associated outputs also agree.
The two original accounts cross at week4 with $26 each.
Teacher reviews graph comparison and contextual reasoning.
